title: An exact projected-angle likelihood and population inversion for wide-binary eccentricities
shortTitle: One angle, an exact likelihood: reading wide-binary eccentricities
oneLine: For wide binary stars seen at a random moment from a random direction, the angle between separation and motion has a closed-form likelihood; its distribution determines the population's eccentricity distribution exactly, and simple averages of the angle estimate eccentricity summaries directly.
abstract: A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. In the ideal model, orbital phase is a random time in the orbit and orientation is uniformly random in three dimensions. For this model the candidate derives the likelihood in closed form, p(γ|e)=[acosh(1/e)−1{|cos γ|>e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)]/(π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for the population law, including atoms, and answers the uniqueness question raised in Appendix B of Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (2022): different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: for example E√(1−e²)=(π/2)E sin³Γ and E e²=1/2+E cos 2Γ−(1/2)E cos 4Γ. These are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets, and they give near-efficient estimators of power-law indices. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a scale-free log-uniform semimajor-axis law. Simulations of Kepler orbits check representative formulas. No observational catalogue is analysed. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Exact likelihood (Theorem 3.1, proof): for eccentricity 0<e<1, p(γ|e)=[acosh(1/e)−1{|cos γ|>e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)]/(π sin²γ); circular orbits give −log|cos γ|/(π sin²γ).

Population inversion (Theorem 4.1, proof): mixtures over any eccentricity law are classical Abel transforms, so the angle law determines the eccentricity law, atoms included, by an explicit inverse. This answers the uniqueness question in Appendix B of Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (2022).
Power laws (Section 5, proof): f(e)=(α+1)e^α gives p_α(γ)=B((α+1)/2,1/2)(1−|cos γ|^(α+1))/(2π sin²γ); a flat angle law forces the thermal law f(e)=2e.

Moments without inversion (Theorems 6.1–6.2, Corollary 7.1, proof): E√(1−e²)=(π/2)E sin³Γ and E e²=1/2+E cos 2Γ−(1/2)E cos 4Γ; each target has at most one symmetric unbiased single-angle observable. Power-law index estimators reach at least 96% efficiency on the computed grid (Section 7.2).

Selection (Propositions 8.1–8.2, proof): thermal populations keep flat angles under selections that ignore sky position angles; binning by projected separation is exact under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law and otherwise reweights by an explicit factor.

Stability limit (Propositions 9.1–9.2, proof): the inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure in the eccentricity law can be nearly invisible in the angles.

narration: Reading the shapes of star orbits from a single angle. An Evidence Press briefing. Many stars live in wide pairs, so far apart that one orbit takes thousands of years. Astronomers would like to know how stretched, or eccentric, these orbits are, because that records how the pairs formed. But nobody can watch a whole orbit. What the Gaia satellite can measure is a snapshot: the line joining the two stars, and the direction in which they are moving relative to each other. The angle between those two directions carries information about the orbit's shape. This release works out that information exactly, for pairs caught at a random moment and seen from a random direction. It gives a short closed formula for how likely each angle is, for an orbit of any eccentricity. It then proves that the full spread of angles across many pairs pins down the spread of eccentricities completely, answering a question raised by Hwang, Ting and Zakamska in 2022. The catch is that fine detail is almost invisible, so in practice only broad features can be recovered. The paper also gives simple averages of the angle that estimate useful summaries directly, such as the average squared eccentricity, and it identifies which common ways of selecting stars keep these results exact. The proofs are written out, and computer simulations of Kepler orbits check the formulas. No real star catalogue is analysed, and real data would need a model of measurement errors. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: The identified set is a single law: closed-form likelihood of the projected separation–velocity angle of a Kepler orbit, and a measure-level Abel inverse showing that the angle law of a population determines its eccentricity law; explicit moment observables, power-law estimators, exact selection results and the stability limit of the inverse.
decisionObject.scope: Ideal model: uniform mean anomaly (or any phase law with the pairing property), Haar-random orientation, error-free projections, i.i.d. observations. Measurement error, general selection and real catalogues are not addressed.

semanticBridge.description: Section 1 quotes Appendix B of Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (2022) and states which part of the question is answered: exact uniqueness for every law; approximate uniqueness weakly but not in total variation. Section 2 fixes the model in the same conventions (uniform mean anomaly, random orientation) as their Section 2.
remainingRisks: The ideal phase and orientation assumptions must hold in the analysed sample; Section 8 identifies the selections that preserve them.
